A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same autoencoder double-descent study despite changes to the title and presentation. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original autoencoder experiments on synthetic data, single-cell RNA, and CelebA, including reconstruction, domain-adaptation, and anomaly-detection outcomes.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds linear-autoencoder controls, image-data experiments, nonlinear synthetic data, and robustness investigations.

M1.justification: V1 uses a single fully connected autoencoder architecture. V2 extends the studied models with convolutional encoders and decoders and a sparse variant retaining the top 500 of 550 embedding coordinates (Appendices A, F.3, and F.6). These substantially expand architecture and latent processing, while retaining the original FCN and self-reconstruction MSE objective.

E1.justification: V2 adds MNIST and CIFAR-10 image experiments, bidirectional MNIST/MNIST-M domain shifts, nonlinear polynomial synthetic data, and reconstruction tests with noisy image inputs. The original linear-subspace, single-cell RNA, and CelebA coverage is retained.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 2 adds a matched linear autoencoder comparator to the nonlinear architecture sweep; v1 Figure 2 evaluates only nonlinear AEs. The downstream comparisons continue to examine AE model sizes rather than introduce evaluated external anomaly-detection or domain-adaptation methods.

E3.justification: V2 introduces CNN channel sweeps, PSNR evaluation of reconstructed images, and KL-divergence measurement of domain shifts. Figure 3 adds 0% noise for synthetic data and 70–90% noise for RNA. CelebA's reported feature count changes from 39 to 40; this documents a setting revision without establishing that the retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test identity learning in overcomplete AEs, robustness to Laplacian noise and sparse embeddings, and noise reduction without explicit denoising training (Figures 34, 37, 57, and 58). Final-ascent investigations extend the isolated upturns already observed in v1. Existing feature-noise analyses largely survive through relocation to Appendix E.

E5.justification: V2 specifies 5–15 random seeds where v1 states at least 5. Both retain ten-seed averaging for Figure 3 and shaded bands representing ±1 standard error. This refines run-count reporting without demonstrating increased repetitions for retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds noise-level curves in Figure 3, linear-AE results, extensive CNN and nonlinear-data results, sparse/Laplacian findings, and MNIST PSNR examples. Figure 12 newly reports domain-shift KLD values, including 0.246 for Wang. The RNA domain-adaptation KNN-DAT result of 0.75 is retained from v1 Figure 17.

T1.justification: V2 adds a generalization-error definition, full-rank training assumption, Theorem 4.2, and Appendix C's proof and Lemma C.2. These establish nonincreasing test error with increasing bottleneck size for optimal linear AEs. V1's mathematical treatment principally supplies SNR calculations, which remain substantially unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add a central analytical and empirical distinction between linear AEs without double descent and nonlinear AEs exhibiting multiple descents. V2 also explicitly extends the claimed scope across architectural designs. The original claims about reconstruction and downstream benefits remain.

C2.justification: V2 attributes the linear/nonlinear contrast to nonlinearity, clarifies how the smallest layer determines the bottleneck, discusses inherent RNA noise, and tentatively connects final ascent to supervised findings. Its limitations shift from reliance on one FCN architecture to dataset scale and computational constraints.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds CelebA sampling and contamination-dependent test-set construction, CNN architecture and hyperparameters, and expanded computational accounting; Appendix F.6 specifies sparse-embedding settings. However, the computational paragraph still counts four RNA noise levels for Figure 3(b), although the revised figure displays seven.

R1.justification: V2 repositions the contribution around fully unsupervised self-reconstruction and the linear/nonlinear distinction, sharpening its relationship to Lupidi et al., PCR, and denoising studies. It substantially expands AE application, architecture, and theoretical references, including Kawaguchi, Eckart and Young, Gao et al., and Xue et al.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, and much of the explanatory prose are rewritten. A linear-AE theory section precedes the reorganized nonlinear results, dataset details move into Appendix A, and feature-noise material is consolidated in Appendix E. These are extensive narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout. Figure 2 combines an architecture diagram with linear/nonlinear heatmaps, existing test/train plots are regrouped across appendices, and Table 1 gains dataset and architecture columns. New displays include the CNN diagram, reconstruction-image grid, and numerous experimental plots.

improvement.justification: V1 acknowledged reliance on one FCN architecture and left theory to future work. V2's conditional theorem and matched linear control clarify a boundary of the phenomenon, while CNN, sparse-AE, and nonlinear/noise experiments substantially strengthen evidence for generality. Reproducibility details also improve. The inconsistent four-level computational count versus seven curves in Figure 3(b) is a localized reporting defect that does not outweigh these scientific gains.
